abstract.p: Despite the success of CAR T therapy in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), recurrence remains challenging. Previously, we showed that ex vivo priming with decitabine (DAC) enhances CAR T persistence and efficacy. Here, we report on an open-label non-randomised phase I/II trial (NCT04697940) evaluating DAC-primed CD19/CD20 dual-targeted CAR T cells (dCAR T) in 23 patients with relapsed or refractory NHL. Primary endpoints are safety and dose-toxicity for phase I, and overall response rate and complete response rate (CRR) for phase II. Secondary endpoints include progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival, and duration of response. This trial has met pre-specified endpoints. Treatment is well tolerated and achieves durable responses, with an 87% CRR and a 2-year PFS of 77% (median follow-up, 24.3 months). Compared with historically unmodified CAR T cohorts, dCAR T cells exhibited robust in vivo expansion and sustained persistence. Single-cell sequencing indicates that DAC priming enriches for memory-like progenitors, which maintain cytotoxic and memory signatures, and upregulates genes associated with T cell fitness and engagement of endogenous immunity. These data establish DAC-priming as a clinically feasible epigenetic reprogramming strategy enhanceing CAR T durability and efficacy, offering a generalizable paradigm for engineered cell therapies in malignant tumors.

Despite the success of CAR T cell-based immunotherapies, patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) face a high risk of recurrence. Here, the authors report clinical outcomes of a phaseI/II study on refractory NHL patients treated with anti-CD19-anti-CD20 CAR T cell product epigenetically reprogrammed with decitabine and CAR T cel properties. In addition, they investigate the persistence and fate of the CAR T cell product, indicating the acquisition of memory-like features, maintained cytotoxicity and reduced exhaustion signature.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, a successful innovation in cancer immunotherapy, has revolutionized the treatment for hematologic malignancies1–6. It is now established as the standard treatment for second-line and subsequent indications and is increasingly being explored for integration into first-line treatment strategies7,8. Despite durable remissions in a subset of patients, therapeutic failures9–12 remain frequent due to insufficient CAR T cell persistence and tumor escape mechanisms13, including antigen loss14,15. Although dual-target CAR T strategies have improved response rates16–19, more than one-third of responders relapse within one year, underscoring the need for novel approaches to overcome resistance.

T cell exhaustion, a state of progressive functional decline driven by chronic antigen stimulation, is a central mechanism of CAR T cell failure15,20–22. Exhausted CAR T cells exhibit a PD-1+TIM3+ phenotype with impaired cytokine secretion (IL-2, TNF, and IFN-γ)22–24 and poor clinical outcomes, as observed in the ZUMA‑7 trial25. Although targeting T cell exhaustion could provide a therapeutic opportunity, combining CAR T cells with immune checkpoint inhibitors against these surface markers has so far yielded limited clinical benefit26,27, indicating that the dysfunction is not merely receptor-mediated but is deeply imprinted at a cellular level. Converging evidence identifies epigenetic dysregulation as a key driver that establishes and maintains the exhausted state28–30; together with preclinical evidence that epigenetic modulators can reverse T-cell dysfunction31–33, and our prior work showing that the hypomethylating agent decitabine (DAC) preserves a memory-like, non-exhausted phenotype in CAR T cells during chronic antigen exposure34, these data suggest that directly targeting the epigenetic machinery itself could be a more effective strategy to restore T cell fitness.

Here, we investigate the clinical efficacy and molecular mechanisms of decitabine-primed CD19/CD20 dual-targeting CAR T cells (dCAR T) in patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell lymphoma. We demonstrate that epigenetic reprogramming with decitabine during CAR T cell manufacturing confers a memory-like phenotype, robust proliferation capacity, and sustained antitumor activity, resulting in high rates of complete response and durable remission. This study establishes epigenetic modulation as a potent strategy to overcome T cell exhaustion and provides a scalable framework for enhancing the therapeutic persistence of engineered T cell therapies in hematological malignancies.

sec.title: Clinical trial design and participants
sec.p: Between 15 April 2021 and 20 August 2024, we conducted a Phase I/II trial at the First Medical Center of the Chinese PLA General Hospital to assess the safety and efficacy of epigenetically modified dual-target CAR T (dCAR T) cells in 23 adult patients with relapsed or refractory NHL. The trial consisted of two parts: Phase I was a dose-escalation study (n = 9) using a standard 3 + 3 design across three dose levels to determine safety, dose-limiting toxicity (DLT), and determination of the recommended phase II dose (RP2D). Phase II was an expansion cohort (n = 14) in which patients received dCAR T cells at the RP2D. The primary efficacy endpoints were overall response rate (ORR) and complete response rate (CRR), while secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), duration of response (DOR), and time to response. The study design and inclusion/exclusion criteria are detailed in the “Methods” section and the Supplementary trial protocol.

A total of 30 patients were screened, of whom seven were excluded (four for not meeting the inclusion criteria, one due to withdrawal of consent, and two owing to failure of pre-culture) (Fig. 1a). Twenty-three patients underwent leukapheresis, successfully manufactured dCAR T-cell products, received infusion, and completed at least 9 months of follow-up. The median age was 52 years (range, 18–75). At enrollment, 83% had stage III–IV disease and 83% had aggressive B-cell lymphoma, including 15 with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL; 67% were double-expressors) and four with other histologies [high-grade B-cell lymphoma (HGBCL), primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (PMBCL), large-cell transformation from follicular lymphoma (FL), and large-cell transformation from marginal zone lymphoma (MZL)]. Extranodal involvement was present in 61%. The median number of prior systemic therapies was three (range, 2–6). Most patients (83%) had primary refractory disease, 87% were non-responsive to their most recent therapy, and all had progressive disease before enrollment. Bulky disease was reported in 22%, and 30% had CD19-negative or weakly CD19-positive tumors. sec.title: Characteristics of dCAR T-cell products
sec.p:
Building on our prior preclinical findings34, in which decitabine treatment during CAR T manufacturing resulted in global DNA hypomethylation alongside decreased DNMT3a protein levels, we assessed DNMT3a expression in dCAR T cells to infer epigenetic modulation. Compared to concurrently cultured control CAR T cells without DAC treatment, dCAR T cells from all 23 patients exhibited reduced DNMT3a expression (mean reduction, 50%; 95% CI, 40.2–61.0) (Fig. 2a). To further validate genome-wide epigenetic remodeling, we performed targeted enzymatic methylation sequencing (Targeted EM-seq) on paired dCAR T and unmodified CAR T cells from five representative patients with sufficient cryopreserved samples. Consistent with the downregulation of DNMT3a, sequencing analysis revealed a global reduction in DNA methylation levels in dCAR T cells compared with their untreated counterparts (Fig. 2b). Notably, dCAR T cells displayed a trend toward hypomethylation across the mitochondrial genome and chromosome 19, while exhibiting significantly decreased methylation across the remaining 21 chromosomes pairs relative to control CAR T cells (Supplementary Fig. 1). The mean transduction efficiency of the CAR gene for dCAR T cells was 25.37% (95% CI, 21.6–29.2), and these cells predominantly displayed a memory phenotype. Stem cell-like memory T cells (TSCM) and central memory T cells (TCM) accounted for mean proportions of 22% (95% CI, 17.2–27.6) and 36% (95% CI, 30.1–42.7), respectively. Furthermore, the proportion of cells co-expressing PD-1 and TIM-3 was low (Fig. 2c). Detailed dCAR T cell product characteristics for each patient are provided in Supplementary Table 3.

sec.title: Safety and tolerability of dCAR T cells
sec.p:
No DLTs were observed in Phase I. Based on safety outcomes, dCAR T kinetics and cost considerations, the RP2D was established at 2 × 106 cells/kg. Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) occurred in 87% of patients, but all were grade 1–2 and manageable; most presented with pyrexia, headache or chills, while two experienced grade 2 hypoxia requiring oxygen owing to effusion (Table 2). CRS developed at a median of 3 days post-infusion and typically lasted 4 days. Serum interleukin (IL)−6, IL-8, and IL-10 showed only modest, non‑significant increases versus baseline and remained near the upper limit of normal (ULN) throughout the 3 months post-infusion (Fig. 3a). Conversely, TNF levels rose significantly during the same period and remained persistently elevated. Relative to the ULN, TNF increased 4.0-fold by day 7 (95% CI: 1.48–6.69) and continued its upward trajectory, peaking at 19.56-fold (95% CI: 4.21–34.92) (Fig. 3b). Grade ≥ 3 toxicities were mainly reversible cytopenias related to lymphodepletion, while other treatment-related events (≥10%) included rash, fatigue, nausea, effusions and “local CRS35” (Table 2). Infections were infrequent, with no grade ≥3 events (Table 2). Details of toxicities for each patient are provided in Supplementary Table 4. Six patients required infliximab, but none required corticosteroids. Neurological events were rare. One patient developed somnolence, confusion, and bulbar conjunctival edema on day 6 post-infusion; because these symptoms occurred following the peak of CRS, the event was classified as grade 2 immune cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) (Table 2). Due to the bulbar conjunctival edema suggestive of cerebral edema, mannitol was administered urgently, and symptoms resolved within 6 h without the need for corticosteroids. Detailed characteristics and interventions for CRS/ICANS are listed in Supplementary Table 5. All patients developed profound B-cell aplasia following dCAR T infusion, coinciding with peripheral CAR T cell expansion (Fig. 3d, e). Spearman correlation analysis demonstrated a significant negative association between CAR T cell expansion and the B-cell counts (rho = −0.61, p = 0.03). Previous studies have demonstrated that persistent B-cell aplasia may serve as a functional surrogate marker for the enduring activity of CAR-T cells36–38. In 15 patients, B-cell aplasia persisted beyond 1 year, and in 10 cases it remained at the last follow-up (Table 3 and Fig. 3d), consistent with sustained CAR T-cell persistence and activity. sec.title: Durable clinical responses after dCAR T cell infusion
sec.p: By the data cutoff date of 31 May 2025, all 23 patients evaluable for 9‑month activity had been followed for a median of 24.3 months (range, 10.1–50.7). Twenty-two patients (96%; 95% CI, 78–100) achieved an objective response, including 20 complete responses (CR, 87%) and 2 partial responses (PR) (Table 3 and Fig. 1b). The median time to CR was 1 month (range, 1–6); four patients who initially achieved PR subsequently converted to CR within 3–6 months (Supplementary Table 6). At the data cutoff, 16 patients (70%) remained in ongoing CR without further therapy (Fig.1b and Supplementary Fig. 2). Three- and six‑month CR rates were 70% and 74%, respectively (Table3). In the phase II cohort, best ORR (93%) and CRR (86%) did not differ significantly from the overall population (p = 0.78).

The high efficacy of dCAR T therapy was maintained across all prespecified high-risk subgroups defined by features known to limit CAR T efficacy in NHL7,39–41, including TP53 mutation, primary refractory disease, high tumor burden, CD19 negativity/weak expression, or history of ≥3 prior therapies (Fig. 1c, d). Median PFS was not reached, with an estimated 2‑year PFS rate of 78% (95% CI, 61–95%), consistent across high‑risk subgroups (Table 3 and Fig. 1e, g). All four patients with follicular lymphoma achieved durable CRs, whereas in the aggressive lymphoma subset (n = 19), the CR rate was 84%, and 74% remained progression‑free at 24 months (Table 3 and Fig. 1f). Median overall survival was not reached (Fig. 1h); the 24‑month OS rate was 88% (95% CI, 72–100%) (Table 3). Among responders, 24‑month duration of response (DOR) and duration of CR (DOCR) were 77% and 85%, respectively (Table 3), with neither the median DOR nor the median DOCR reached (Fig. 1i, j). Phase I and II cohorts showed comparable PFS, OS, and DOR (Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. 3).
At the data cutoff, three deaths had occurred: two from disease progression and one due to sepsis following chemotherapy for a secondary breast cancer, unrelated to dCAR T cell therapy.

sec.title: Enhanced expansion, persistence, and endogenous immune activation of dCAR T cells
sec.p:
CAR T dynamics in peripheral blood were monitored by flow cytometry and qPCR for the CAR transgene until relapse or data cutoff. All 23 patients demonstrated marked in vivo expansion following infusion, with peak CAR T levels reaching 5144 cells/µl and a median of 308 cells/µl (95% CI, 216–1272) (Figs. 3e, 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4). The median persistence level at day 300 was 14 cells/µl, detectable in 17 of 23 patients (Fig. 3e). At peak expansion, CAR-positive T cells comprised up to 88% of circulating T cells (median 43%), occurring at a median of 11 days (range, 7–29) post‑infusion (Fig. 4b). To directly evaluate the effect of epigenetic reprogramming, we compared expansion kinetics to a previously published historical cohort (TanCAR7, n = 82) treated at the same institution using an identical CAR design, manufacturing protocol, and evaluation criteria. dCAR T cells showed significantly increased expansion during the first 10 days post‑infusion (Fig. 4d). As tumor burden can influence expansion, we derived an “efficacy‑to‑target ratio” (E:T) defined as CAR T cell level per tumor burden. Both peak and cumulative E:T ratios were substantially higher with dCAR T cell products than with TanCAR7 products (Fig. 4e), and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated significant discriminatory power (AUC 0.67–0.69; Fig. 4f). Notably, endogenous CD8⁺ T‑cell counts expanded rapidly following dCAR T cell infusion and remained elevated beyond 6 months (Fig. 4g). In four patients, synchronous re‑expansion of CAR T and endogenous CD8⁺ T cells coincided with transient rises in CD19⁺ B cells (Fig. 4h), implying that dCAR T therapy may amplify endogenous antitumor immunity in addition to direct tumor clearance.

To further dissect mechanisms of epigenetic reprogramming, we performed droplet‑based 5′ single‑cell RNA‑seq (scRNA-seq) on CAR T products from 11 patients in this study (6 with durable response [DOR], 4 with relapse and 1 with stable disease) and 5 from the TanCAR7 trial (3 DOR, 2 progression). Clustering identified 16 transcriptionally distinct subsets (Fig. 5a). Compared with TanCAR7, dCAR T cells were enriched in CD8⁺ effector/central memory and CD4⁺ effector memory clusters, with a striking accumulation within cytotoxic CD4⁺ populations that were rarely observed in TanCAR7 (Fig. 5b). Consistent with DAC‑mediated demethylation, dCAR T cells exhibited reduced expression of DNA methylation regulators (including DNMT1, DNMT3A, and UHRF1), alongside increased transcription of genes linked to proliferation, memory maintenance and cytokine signaling. CD40LG expression was markedly upregulated, a feature associated with enhanced engagement of endogenous immunity (Fig. 5c). Gene set enrichment analyses corroborated these findings, showing downregulation of methylation pathways and heterogeneous activation of immune effector, cytokine, and receptor signaling programs (Fig. 5d).

To determine whether these transcriptional changes were directly driven by epigenetic modulation, we analyzed differentially methylated regions (DMRs) using Targeted EM-seq data from the 5 paired dCAR T and control CAR T samples. Consistent with the global hypomethylation profile, dCAR T cells displayed significant epigenetic remodeling compared with unmodified controls (Fig. 5e). Crucially, this remodeling involved targeted hypomethylation of genes encoding DNA methyltransferases as well as key regulators of T cell memory and effector function. Specifically, we observed decreased methylation levels in the loci of DNMT3A, JUN, RUNX3, TCF7, LEF1, PRPTC, and ZNF683 (Fig. 5f), aligning with their observed transcriptional upregulation or functional relevance in promoting memory and cytotoxicity.

Together, these data demonstrate that decitabine modification enhances the magnitude and persistence of CAR T cell expansion, improves the balance between effector function and tumor load, and promotes endogenous T‑cell responses through epigenetic reprogramming.

sec.title: Memory-like progenitors drive oligoclonal expansion of dCAR T Cells
sec.p:
To delineate the dynamics of TCR repertoires and transcriptomes in dCAR T cells across in vivo expansion and contraction phases, we performed droplet‑based 5′ scRNA‑seq coupled with paired TCR sequencing (scTCR‑seq). Samples included infusion dCAR T products (IDP) from nine patients, as well as circulating dCAR T cells at peak expansion (day 7–14, Peak) and contraction phases (day 26–42, Late). Shannon diversity indices indicated a marked reduction in CD8⁺ dCAR T clonal diversity post‑infusion (Fig. 6a). Following infusion, the proportion of the top 10 clonotypes within the CD8 + CAR T cell population progressively increased during the Peak and Late phases relative to IDP (Fig. 6b and Supplementary Fig. 5). In only four patients did these dominant IDP clonotypes remain highly ranked post‑infusion, whereas in most patients the top in vivo clones arose from low-frequency IDP clones (Fig. 6c–f). Moreover, clonal hierarchies were stable from Peak to Late, suggesting that oligoclonal expansion, rather than transient polyclonal bursts, drives long‑term persistence.Fig. 6Clonal architecture and dynamics of dCAR T cells.

Across 57,747 CAR T cells identified by CAR transgene mapping and combining TCRα/β chain tracking, unsupervised clustering and UMAP visualization showed that both CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ dCAR‑T cells at Peak and Late stages diverged transcriptionally from the IDP, but remained overlapping with each other (Fig. 7a, b). Principal-component analysis corroborated this, demonstrating significant drift from IDP to in vivo states but minimal differences between Peak and Late (Fig. 4c). Compared with IDP cells, in vivo dCAR T cells upregulated effector‑associated regulators (RUNX3, TBX21, and STAT1) and cytotoxic molecules (GZMH, GZMM, and NKG7), while maintaining stable expression of memory‑associated genes (SELL, TCF7, IL7R, and PRDM1) (Fig. 7d). Exhaustion markers (TIGIT, LAG3, ENTPD1, and LGALS3) and epigenetic regulators (DNMT1 and UHRF1) remained consistently low (Fig. 7d). CD8⁺ dCAR T cells in vivo exhibited higher activation, IFN‑γ response, cytotoxicity and memory scores relative to CD8⁺ IDP cells, with no decline between Peak and Late (Fig. 7e). CD4⁺ dCAR T cells, in contrast, showed progressive enrichment of memory signatures post‑infusion (Fig. 7f). Both subsets displayed lower glycolytic and exhaustion scores than their IDP counterparts. Finally, by linking clonal fate to transcriptional identity, we identified a definitive signature of the successful progenitor cells. We traced the dominant in vivo clonotypes back to their origins within the infusion product and found that they arose from cells with a distinct transcriptional state (Fig. 7g). Unlike the most abundant clones in the IDP (Fig. 7g), which were already highly proliferative and expressed high levels of effector molecules (GZMA, GZMB, and MKI67), the progenitors of the winning clones were defined by a quiescent, memory-like signature. They were distinguished by high expression of genes central to T-cell memory and survival, including IL7R, KLF2, and CD44, coupled with low expression of effector and proliferation markers (Fig. 7h, i). These data suggest that the durable antitumor response originates not from the most active cells in the infusion product, but from a less differentiated, quiescent subset poised for superior fitness, expansion and persistence upon antigen encounter in vivo.

Collectively, these findings establish that epigenetic programming of dCAR T cells favors the emergence of memory‑like clones capable of oligoclonal dominance, sustained effector function, and resistance to exhaustion, which may underpin the enhanced persistence and clinical durability observed.

sec.title: Analysis of factors related to dCAR T therapy failure
sec.p: Finally, we examined determinants of dCAR T therapy failure. Only one patient (UPN21, HGBCL) showed no clinical response and showed no clinical response (stable disease). Serial PET-CT at 3, 6, and 12 months showed no evidence of progression, and the patient remained off therapy at data cutoff (Supplementary Fig. 2). Five additional patients relapsed after initial response: two patients (UPN3 and UPN16) relapsed after maintaining a PR for 3 months, and three patients (UPN15, UPN17, and UPN20) relapsed after maintaining a CR for 3–6 months. Among these, three lost CD19/CD20 expression after infusion (Supplementary Fig. 6). Pre-infusion tumors from UPN15, UPN17 and UPN20 exhibited low NOXA (Supplementary Fig. 7), previously linked to poor CAR T therapy outcomes42; all five relapse patients carried at least three predefined risk factors (Supplementary Fig. 8).

Analysis of infusion products showed that sustained responders harbored relatively higher CD8⁺ and TEFF contents, whereas relapsed patients exhibited lower representation of these functional subsets, though TEFF proportions remained <10% in both groups (Supplementary Fig. 9). Single-cell RNA-seq from nine patients revealed 14 shared transcriptional clusters with broadly comparable distributions (Supplementary Fig. 10), indicating no drastic differences in lineage composition. In vivo, CAR T expansion, persistence, AUC, E:T ratios and CD4/CD8 balance were largely similar, except for UPN15, who displayed profoundly limited expansion (13.1 cells/µL, versus an average of 744 cells/µL; Supplementary Fig. 11). Laboratory monitoring revealed no group differences in IL-2, WBC recovery, or peripheral CD4/CD8 balance. By contrast, sustained responders exhibited consistently higher serum TNF in early follow-up, reaching significance at day 3 (Supplementary Fig. 12), consistent with their greater CD8⁺ TEFF content.

Together, these findings suggest that relapse after dCAR T therapy arises from the interplay of tumor-intrinsic factors (such as antigen loss, low NOXA) and product-related deficiencies (reduced CD8⁺/TEFF representation), rather than from systemic persistence failure.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In real-world practice, CD19-directed CAR T therapy achieves ORRs of 57–80% in B-cell lymphomas, but only 30–40% of patients experience durable remission, with more than half of initial responders relapsing within one year6,9–12,43. Such relapses are frequently mediated by antigen escape or limited CAR T persistence. To address this, tandem CAR constructs targeting CD19/CD20 or CD19/CD22 have been developed, yielding CR rates of 50–88% and 6‑month and 2‑year PFS rates of 55–80% and 40–65%, respectively; however, relapse rates by two years still approach 50%16,19,44,45. Here, we show that transient ex vivo epigenetic reprogramming of CD19/CD20 tandem CAR T cells with decitabine (dCAR T) induces rapid, deep, and remarkably durable responses in patients with relapsed or refractory NHL. dCAR T achieved a CR rate of 87% and a 24‑month PFS of 78%, substantially outperforming historical outcomes with unmodified tandem CAR T (TanCAR7, 6‑ and 12‑month PFS of 69% and 61%, respectively17,46), which utilized an identical CAR construct and manufacturing platform. This direct comparison allows us to conclude that the enhanced durability stems from the epigenetic reprogramming itself, rather than from the dual targeting alone. Importantly, dCAR T also demonstrated benefit in high-risk subsets39,47, including TP53-mutated, double-expressor DLBCL and bulk tumor burden, settings where conventional CAR T responses are typically attenuated. Toxicity was manageable: cytokine release syndrome occurred in 87% of patients but was predominantly grade 1 and controlled with standard interventions. Notably, despite marked in vivo expansion, we did not observe an increase in high-grade toxicities, distinguishing dCAR T from armored or cytokine-secreting CAR designs that often amplify inflammatory risks48–50. Nonetheless, longer follow-up and larger studies will be essential to validate the durability of clinical benefit and to exclude late-onset toxicities or immune dysregulation.

Consistent with the clinical benefit findings, dCAR T cells achieved robust in vivo expansion and durable persistence. Flow cytometry and qPCR revealed striking levels of early expansion, with CAR-positive cells accounting for nearly half of the peripheral T cell pool and remaining detectable for up to 300 days. Although peak expansion and AUC were not significantly different between dCAR T and TanCAR7 cohorts, the E:T ratio was consistently superior in dCAR T. This metric, integrating CAR‑T cell numbers with tumor burden, suggests that epigenetic modulation yields a functionally more potent T‑cell product, better poised to balance proliferative fitness against antigen load. Of particular note, dCAR T infusion was accompanied by a coordinated expansion of endogenous CD8⁺ T cells, in several cases re-expanding synchronously with CAR T upon transient B‑cell recovery. Such reciprocal activation was not observed with TanCAR7, raising the hypothesis that dCAR T not only mediates direct cytotoxicity but also acts as a facilitator of host immune re-engagement, potentially replenishing tumor surveillance mechanisms after CAR‑T contraction.

The transcriptional programs delineated by scRNA-seq provide mechanistic insights into the above observations. Compared to TanCAR7, dCAR T cells were enriched for CD8⁺ TCM/TEM and cytotoxic CD4⁺ subsets, lineages previously linked to long-term persistence and proliferative reserve13,40,51–54. Interestingly, we identified a profound enrichment of a cytotoxic CD4⁺ T cell population, a cell type with potent, MHC class II-dependent tumor-killing capabilities that was largely absent in the conventional CAR T product. The selective reduction of methylation pathway genes (DNMT1, DNMT3A and UHRF1) in dCAR T cells, together with the upregulation of memory- and cytokine-related pathways, suggests that epigenetic modulation efficiently rewires differentiation trajectories away from terminal effector states. The overexpression of CD40LG in dCAR T products further implicates enhanced costimulatory capacity, which could underlie activation of bystander endogenous lymphocytes and foster a more polyclonal immune response.

Epigenetically primed dCAR T cells exhibit a trajectory that diverges from the canonical dynamics described for conventional anti-CD19 CAR T therapy. Previous longitudinal single-cell studies of infused anti-CD19 CAR T products demonstrated an early, highly polyclonal burst dominated by terminal effector populations that rapidly contract and acquire exhaustion hallmarks, limiting long-term persistence55. A distinct but related framework has recently been reported, where durable remissions correlated not with CAR T clones per se, but with robust activation and clonotypic expansion of the endogenous cytotoxic T cell compartment56. Together, these studies highlight the inherent instability of effector-skewed CAR T expansions and the critical involvement of host immunity in shaping long-term outcomes. By contrast, our integrative scRNA/TCR analyses revealed that dCAR T persistence is driven by oligoclonal dominance of progenitors with a memory‑like transcriptional state, rather than transient proliferation of abundant effector clones. Notably, the dominant clones arising in vivo frequently originated from rare, quiescent subsets in the infusion product, enriched for IL7R, KLF2, and CD44 but low in MKI67 and effector transcripts, a profile resembling TSCM cells. This is consistent with the notion that less differentiated progenitors provide the stem for both early expansion and long-term clonal maintenance, a mechanism also supported by independent clinical evidence that TSCM‑derived clones disproportionately contribute to long-lived CAR T populations and sustained anti-leukemic surveillance57.

Unlike conventional anti-CD19 CAR T cells that progressively lose diversity and accumulate exhaustion signatures over time55, dCAR T clones preserved transcriptional hallmarks of long-lived memory (such as TCF7 and PRDM1) while maintaining effector competence (RUNX3 and TBX21) and limiting exhaustion marker expression. These transcriptional features are supported by epigenetic evidence from targeted EM-seq, which revealed significantly reduced methylation levels at key memory-, effector- and exhaustion-related loci in dCAR T cells compared to conventional CAR T counterparts. This provides a mechanistic basis for stable expression of functional genes and contributes to the maintenance of durable memory states. This balance likely reflects decitabine-induced epigenetic rewiring, which appears to bias fate decisions toward progenitor‑memory states, endowing superior clonal fitness and resistance to exhaustion. This hypothesis is consistent with previous preclinical observations from our group showing that exposure to decitabine promotes memory phenotypes and sustained demethylation in CAR T cells in both in vitro and murine models34. Although longitudinal chromatin accessibility or methylome profiling at the single-cell level could not be performed on in vivo samples in this cohort due to limited cell recovery, we speculate that DAC modulates epigenetic fate commitment by interfering with de novo methylation events that otherwise reinforce exhaustion and restrict memory differentiation. Indeed, a body of evidence suggests that exhaustion-prone effector T cells acquire site-specific DNA methylation that locks them in dysfunctional states, and that pharmacologic hypomethylation can delay or even partially reverse this trajectory31,58,59.

Thus, dCAR T dynamics resemble a “programmed oligoclonality” rooted in epigenetically stabilized memory‑like cells, contrasting sharply with the effector-driven short-lived expansions documented in conventional CAR T trials. Collectively, these findings suggest that transient epigenetic priming establishes a developmental hierarchy that reconciles effector function with long-term persistence. This decitabine‑induced rewiring of the developmental hierarchy appears to bias CAR T fate towards memory-biased oligoclonality, thereby reconciling effector potency with long-term persistence. This dynamics, characterized by memory-driven oligoclonal expansion, transcriptionally active low-exhaustion persistent populations; this dynamics may be key to maintaining long-term antitumor effects, and provide a mechanistic basis for the superior clinical durability of dCAR T compared with conventional or even bispecific CAR T products.

Analysis of treatment failures further elucidated the critical interplay between cellular product and tumor biology. Consistent with previous reports, intrinsic tumor resistance mechanisms, most notably antigen loss, even under dual targeting strategies, remain a major driver of relapse14,60. Moreover, we observed that patients who experienced early relapse harbored dCAR T infusion products with a reduced proportion of CD8⁺ effector T cells compared with those achieving durable remission. This deficiency was paralleled by a blunted early inflammatory response (lower TNF levels), suggesting that while a memory progenitor pool is essential for long-term persistence, an initial, robust pro-inflammatory burst orchestrated by effector cells may be crucial for achieving deep and durable tumor clearance, a concept supported by prior studies linking early cytokine profiles to clinical outcomes13,61.

Our study has limitations. The comparisons with historical cohorts, while informative, cannot substitute for the rigor of randomized trials. Furthermore, as all patients were treated at a single center, the encouraging safety and durability signals observed here require validation in larger, multicenter clinical studies to establish generalizability.

In conclusion, our trial demonstrates both the safety and sustained efficacy of dCAR T therapy in r/r NHL. The strategy of ex vivo decitabine priming enables epigenetic reprogramming of CAR T cells, providing not only a mechanistic basis for their enhanced persistence but also proposing a new paradigm with broad applicability for the preparation of engineered cell products.

sec.title: Clinical trial design
sec.p: This trial was conducted in accordance with the International Conference on Harmonization Good Clinical Practice guidelines and the Declaration of Helsinki. All patients provided written informed consent. Approval for the protocol and use of human samples was granted by the Ethics Committee of the Chinese PLA General Hospital (Identifier Number: S2020-029-058/S2021-006-01).

This was an open-label, single-center, single-cohort Phase I/II clinical trial evaluating the feasibility, safety, and preliminary efficacy of dCAR T cells in patients with r/r NHL (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04697940). The Phase I portion followed a standard 3 + 3 dose-escalation design at three dose levels: DL1 (0.5 × 106 CAR T cells/kg), DL2 (2.0 × 106 CAR T cells/kg), and DL3 (5.0 × 106 CAR T cells/kg). Up to six patients could be enrolled per cohort. A dose level was considered safe once at least three patients had received the target dose and completed the 30-day DLT assessment without meeting predefined DLT criteria. DLTs were defined as: (1) Any grade ≥3 non-hematologic toxicity attributable to dCAR T cells that failed to resolve to grade ≤2 within 14 days; (2) Grade 4 CRS or neurotoxicity, or grade 3 neurotoxicity persisting for >72 h; (3) Any treatment-related event requiring intubation; (4) Any fatal (grade 5) or other life-threatening (grade 4) uncontrolled toxicity; (5) Any toxicity necessitating protocol amendment, as determined by the investigators or the Safety Review Committee. Following dose escalation, the RP2D for cohort expansion was selected to optimize therapeutic index, balancing anti-tumor activity, tolerability, manufacturing feasibility, and clinical practicality. Phase II consisted of an expansion cohort treated at the RP2D to formally assess safety and preliminary efficacy.

sec.title: Patient eligibility
sec.p: The main inclusion criteria are designed to include: (1) Age ≥ 18 and ≤75 years. (2) Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status score between 0 and 2. (3) Life expectancy > 3 months. (4) Histologically confirmed CD20+ and/or CD19 + B-cell lymphoma, according to the World Health Organization 2016 classification criteria. (5) Relapse after treatment with ≥2 lines of systemic therapy for all B-cell lymphomas, or primary refractory disease for aggressive types (DLBCL, PMBCL, TFL, HGBCL, et al.). Relapse disease was defined as disease progression after the last regimen. Refractory disease was defined as no CR to first-line therapy: progressive disease (PD) as the best response to first-line therapy, or SD as the best response after at least 4 cycles of first-line therapy, or PR as the best response after at least 6 cycles with biopsy-proven residual disease or disease progression ≤6 months after therapy. Previous autologous HCT was considered as a line of therapy, needed to define disease progression or relapse less than or equal to 12 months after transplantation. (6) According to the Lugano response criteria 2014, there should be at least one evaluable tumor focus. An evaluable tumor focus was defined as having the longest diameter of intranodal focus > 1.5 cm, or the longest diameter of extranodal focus > 1.0 cm, assessed by computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). (7) Adequate organ function, as detailed in the protocol.

The main exclusion criteria are designed to include: (1) Central nervous system (CNS) invasion or a history of clinically significant CNS diseases (e.g., epilepsy, cerebrovascular diseases) during the screening period. (2) Women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, or who do not agree to use effective contraception during treatment and during the subsequent 1 year. (3) History of allogeneic HCT, or organ transplantation. (4) Patients with primary immunodeficiency or autoimmune diseases requiring immunosuppressive therapy. (5) Patients who received any immunocellular therapy within 6 months before enrollment. (6) Patients who participated in other clinical trials within 4 weeks prior to enrollment. (7) Uncontrolled infectious diseases or other serious illnesses, including but not limited to infections [e.g., human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection or acute or chronic active hepatitis B (HBV) or C (HCV) infection], congestive heart failure, unstable angina, arrhythmias, or that pose an unpredictable risk in the opinion of the attending physician. (8) Inability to understand or unwillingness to sign informed consent.

sec.title: Preconditioning and bridging therapy
sec.p: Patients underwent leukapheresis, followed by FC lymphodepletion regimen with cyclophosphamide (300–500 mg/m2) and fludarabine (25–30 mg/m2) administered on days −5, −4, and −3 before dCAR T cells infusion. In addition, mechlorethamine hydrochloride (4-6 mg/m2 for 1 day) could be considered to bridge the following FC regimen in patients with bulky tumor burden, rapidly aggressive progression, and/or indications of urgent symptom control.

sec.title: Disease assessment
sec.p: CRS and ICANS were graded according to American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) consensus criteria62, and other adverse events (AEs) were assessed per the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 5.0. All AEs, whether observed directly or patient-reported, were monitored from leukapheresis through 3 months post-infusion. Extended surveillance for predefined AEs of interest, including neurological events, cytopenias, infections, autoimmune phenomena, and secondary malignancies, continued for up to 24 months or until disease progression.

Tumor response was evaluated by positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) at baseline, and at 1, 3-, 6-, 12-, and 24-months post-infusion, using the 2014 Lugano classification. Best overall response was categorized as CR, PR, SD, or PD, according to published Lugano criteria. DOR was defined as the interval from the first documented CR or PR until progression, relapse, or death. PFS was defined as the time from dCAR T-cell infusion to progression, relapse, death, or last follow-up. OS was defined as the time from infusion to death from any cause or last follow-up.

sec.title: Sample size
sec.p: The sample size determination was based on a traditional “3 + 3” dose-escalation design in Phase I, followed by a Simon’s two-stage optimal design in Phase II. For the Phase II portion, we assumed a CRR of 50% with existing CD19-directed CAR T cell therapy in relapsed/refractory non-Hodgkin lymphoma (r/r NHL)9, and hypothesized an improvement to 85% with intravenous administration of dCAR T cells. This design provided 80% power to distinguish between true response rates of 50% and 85%, with a one-sided type I error of 0.05. In the first stage, 6 patients were treated with dCAR T cells and evaluated for efficacy. If ≤3 CRs were observed, the trial would be terminated for futility. If ≥4 CRs were achieved, the trial would proceed to the second stage, in which an additional 7 patients were enrolled (for a total of 13 patients). At the end of stage two, if ≥10 of 13 patients achieved CR, the treatment was considered to have met the predefined efficacy criterion and efficacy endpoint.

sec.title: dCAR T cell manufacturing
sec.p: The dCAR T cells utilized in this trial express a tandem CAR targeting CD19 and CD20, which is structurally identical to the TanCAR7 construct used in the NCT03097770 trial. The manufacturing protocol for CAR T cells and the method for low-dose decitabine modification were performed as previously described34,46. Briefly, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from patients. T cells were activated with Dynabeads Human T-Activator CD3/CD28 (Invitrogen; Cat#11131D). Following activation, T cells were transduced with a lentiviral vector encoding the tandem CAR in the presence of 10 μM 5-aza-2′-deoxycytidine (DAC; Sigma; Cat#A3656). After 24 h, T cells infected with the lentiviral vector and modified with DAC were harvested and expanded for 10–14 days. Detailed procedures for manufacturing and quality control assays are described in the study protocol.

sec.title: CD19, CD20, and NOXA immunohistochemistry
sec.p: The intensity of immunohistochemical staining (anti-CD19 antibody, ZSGB-BIO, Cat#ZM-0038; anti-CD20 antibody, ZSGB-BIO, Cat#ZM-0039; NOXA Monoclonal Antibody, Invitrogen, Cat#MA1-41000) was graded to evaluate the expression level as 1, 2, or 3 and then multiplied by the percentage of cells that were positive at each level, as shown in the following formula:
CD19 or CD20 expression score = [1 × (% cells 1+) + 2 × (% cells 2+) + 3 × (% cells 3+)]
A CD19 or CD20 expression score of zero was considered negative.
CD19 and/or CD20 positivity were evaluated by a trained pathologist.
Definition of IHC scoring:

A staining index (0–12) was calculated by multiplying the staining intensity score (0–3) by the positive area score (0–4). A score of 0–7 was defined as low/weak expression, while 8–12 was defined as high expression.
Intensity (0–3): 0 (negative), 1 (weak), 2 (moderate), 3 (strong).

NOXA staining was localized to the cytoplasm of tumor cells and scored according to intensity (0/1/2/3) and positive rate (grouped into quartiles (0–4)). The intensity and positive scores were multiplied to form an IHC score. Low expression scores ranged from 0 to 4, and the scores that exceeded 4 were identified as high expression63.

sec.title: Flow cytometry analysis
sec.p: For CAR expression staining, CAR T cells or peripheral blood samples were incubated with a biotin-SP-AffiniPure F(ab)’2 fragment-specific goat anti-mouse IgG antibody (Jackson ImmunoResearch; Cat#115-066-006), followed by incubation with streptavidin-phycoerythrin (BD Biosciences; PE; Cat#554061) or streptavidin-fluorescein isothiocyanate (BD Biosciences; FITC; Cat#554060). Additional immunophenotyping used pre-titrated anti-human antibodies from BD Biosciences and BioLegend: CD3(PerCP and APC; Cat#552851 and Cat#555335), CD4 (FITC; Cat#550628), CD8 (PE and PerCP; Cat#555367 and Cat#347314), CD45RA (APC; Cat#550855), CD62L (PE; Cat#555544), PD-1 (APC; Cat#558694), TIM3 (PE; Cat#563422) and LAG3 (FITC; BioLegend; Cat#369210). All antibodies were purchased from BD Biosciences unless otherwise specified. Isotype-matched monoclonal antibodies were used as controls for all staining procedures. FACS data were analyzed by a FACS Calibur flow cytometer (BD Biosciences) and FlowJo software (Version 10.0.7, FlowJo, Ashland, OR).

sec.title: Measurement of serum cytokine levels
sec.p: Serum samples were collected from patients at specified time points. The concentrations of TNF (R&D Systems; Cat#DTA00D), IL-2 (R&D Systems; Cat#D2050), IL-6 (R&D Systems; Cat#D6050), IL-8 (R&D Systems; Cat#D8000C), and IL-10 (R&D Systems; Cat#D1000B) were quantified using commercial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Quantitative PCR
sec.p: CAR transgene levels were quantified by real-time PCR as previously described46. A 153-bp fragment containing portions of the CD8a chain and the adjacent 4-1BB chain was amplified using the forward primer 5’-GGTCCTTCTCCTGTCACTGGTT-3’ and reverse primer 5’-TCTTCTTCTTCTGGAAATCGGCAG-3’. Absolute quantification of CAR transgene copy number was performed using a seven-point standard curve (102–108 copies/mL) generated by spiking serial dilutions of the CAR-encoding plasmid into 100 ng of non-transduced control genomic DNA. β-Actin amplification served as an internal control for DNA normalization.

sec.title: Detection of DNMT3a
sec.p: DNMT3a protein levels were analyzed by western blotting. CAR T and dCAR T cells were lysed in RIPA buffer (Cell Signaling Technology; Cat#9806) containing protease inhibitors (Beyotime; Cat#P1005). Protein concentrations were determined using the Bio-Rad assay. After separation on 4–12% SDS-PAGE gels (GenScript; Cat#M00653), proteins were transferred to membranes and probed with anti-DNMT3a (Abcam; Cat#ab2850; 1:20001:2000) and anti-β-actin (Abcam; Cat#ab8226; 1:1000) antibodies.

sec.title: Targeted enzymatic methylation sequencing
sec.p: Genomic DNA extracted from CAR T samples was quantified using a Qubit Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and assessed for quality. High-quality genomic DNA was subjected to library preparation using the Twist NGS Methylation Detection System combined with NEBNext Enzymatic Methyl-seq (EM-seq) (Twist Bioscience), following the manufacturer’s instructions. Unlike traditional bisulfite conversion, this enzymatic approach utilizes a two-step process: oxidation of 5-methylcytosine (5mC) and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) by TET2, followed by deamination of unmethylated cytosines by APOBEC, thereby minimizing DNA damage.

Post-conversion DNA underwent end-repair, A-tailing, and ligation with Illumina-compatible adapters. The ligation products were purified using magnetic beads to remove unligated adapters and short fragments. Libraries were amplified using a high-fidelity DNA polymerase under optimized cycling conditions and subsequently purified. Library quality was validated using a Fragment Analyzer for size distribution and Qubit for quantification.

Target enrichment was performed using the Twist Target Enrichment Kit. Libraries were hybridized with biotinylated capture probes (Twist Bioscience) under constant temperature to ensure specificity. Streptavidin-coated Twist Purification Beads were used to capture the hybridized DNA. Following stringent washing, the captured libraries were eluted and amplified by PCR. The final libraries were purified, pooled, and sequenced on an Illumina Novaseq™ X Plus platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) with a paired-end 150 bp (PE150) configuration.

sec.title: Methylation data analysis
sec.p: Sequencing reads were quality-filtered using Cutadapt and FastQC, then aligned to the reference genome (hg38) using Bismark. PCR duplicates were removed using SAMtools. Methylation levels were determined using MethPipe, and differentially methylated regions (DMRs) were identified using the methylKit R package using a 1000 bp sliding window approach (P < 0.05). Regions (DMRs) were identified using the R package methylKit (v1.8.1). The genome was tiled into 1000 bp sliding windows with a step size of 500 bp. DMRs were defined based on a significance threshold of P < 0.05 using the default parameters of the package.

sec.title: Single-cell RNA and V(D)J sequencing
sec.p: For peripheral blood samples, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated using a lymphocyte separation medium (TBD; Cat#LTS1077) and subsequently prepared as single-cell suspensions in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). dCAR T cell products were directly resuspended in PBS to a final concentration of 2 × 106 cells/mL. Single-cell suspensions were loaded onto a 10× Genomics Chromium Controller, targeting a capture of 8000–10,000 cells per sample. Single-cell gene expression (GEX) and V(D)J libraries were generated using the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Kit (v3) (10x genomics; Cat#PN-1000075) and the Chromium Single Cell V(D)J Enrichment Kit (10× genomics; Cat#PN-1000005), respectively, according to the manufacturer’s protocols. All libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (150 bp, paired-end) by LC-Bio Technology Co., Ltd. (Hangzhou, China) to a minimum depth of 20,000 reads per cell.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using Prism 10 (GraphPad) Software and IBM SPSS Statistics 22. All adverse events were graded according to CTCAE version 5.0 and analyzed via frequency distributions, tables or other descriptive indicators. Statistical significance between two independent groups was assessed using unpaired two-sided t-tests. Normally distributed data were analyzed by Welch’s t-test or unpaired two-sided t-tests, while non-normally distributed data were compared using the Wilcoxon-Mann–Whitney U test. For grouped comparisons from the same TCR clonotype, the two-tailed Student’s t-test was used to test statistical significance for comparisons of two groups. A P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Exact methods [Clopper–Pearson 95% confidence intervals (CIs)] were used for categorical variables. Forest plots include CIs both for individual groups and for the difference between the groups and the reference group. The time of the dCAR T cell infusion was used as the origin in the time-to-event analyses of PFS and OS. PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and were compared with the use of the log-rank test. Differences between the two categories with respect to continuous parameters were determined using an exact Wilcoxon rank sum test. The area under the ROC curve was calculated to evaluate the sensitivity of the multi-index in predicting response or recurrence to dCAR T cell therapy.
